Bernhard Riemann. A German mathematician from eighteen twenty-six to eighteen sixty-six who made groundbreaking contributions to analysis, number theory, and differential geometry. He defined the first rigorous integration theory using what we now call Riemann sums, approximating the area under a curve with rectangular partitions over a closed interval. This rigorous definition became the basis for all modern calculus. He introduced Riemann surfaces, one-dimensional complex manifolds that allow multi-valued functions like the complex logarithm to be treated as single-valued holomorphic functions.

His habilitation lecture, delivered in eighteen fifty-four under Carl Friedrich Gauss's direct supervision, was titled "On the Hypotheses which lie at the Bases of Geometry." This lecture established Riemannian geometry, which generalises geometry to arbitrary dimensions and curved spaces. It introduces the Riemann curvature tensor and defines the metric properties of manifolds, allowing us to measure distances and angles on curved surfaces. This framework later provided the precise mathematical language that Einstein needed for his general relativity.

He formulated the Riemann hypothesis, the most famous conjecture in mathematics: all non-trivial zeroes of the zeta function have a real part equal to one half. This conjecture is central to understanding the distribution of prime numbers and remains one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics today, with a prize of one million dollars for its solution. In an eighteen fifty-nine paper, he laid the analytical foundations for proving the prime number theorem.

He also introduced the Riemann-Roch theorem, which relates the topological genus of a Riemann surface to its algebraic properties. These contributions fundamentally shaped how we understand curves, surfaces, and the deep connection between topology and algebra.
